title: Slide 1 · How do machines learn from examples?
question: A music app predicts which song you will play next. What could it learn from your past listening?
answer: Which songs you played, skipped or replayed give it examples of your preferences.

title: Slide 2 · Every day, we make decisions using patterns.
question: What could an inbox filter predict about a new message?
answer: It could predict whether the message is spam. Examples of messages already marked as spam give it something to learn from.
variants: How can previously labeled emails help a spam filter classify a new message?
How would emails that someone already marked as spam help an inbox filter learn what to do with a new message?
In the inbox example, how would previously labeled emails help a machine learning model make a prediction?

title: Slide 3 · Instead of writing every rule, learn useful parameters from examples.
question: Our score rule gives 10 points per hour. What would make that number a learned weight?
answer: Use past study records and scores to adjust the number according to how well the rule predicts.

title: Slide 4 · Can study patterns help predict a practice score?
question: Which two facts about Ava are available before the quiz? What do we want to predict?
answer: We know her study hours and completed practice sets. Her quiz score is the outcome we want to predict.

title: Slide 5 · Three examples give us something to work with.
question: Ava completes a fourth practice set. Which entry in her record changes?
answer: Her practice-set entry goes from 3 to 4. Her hours remain 2, so her new row is [2, 4].

title: Slide 6 · Collect → Represent → Predict → Compare → Improve.
question: Which step first requires the actual quiz scores?
answer: Comparison. To measure a prediction error, we need both the prediction and the score that was observed.

title: Slide 7 · Give each number a name before writing code.
question: Keep the three sets and change hours from 2 to 3. What will print?
answer: 65. One additional hour adds 10 points to the original 55.

title: Slide 8 · Now turn our story into a computation.
question: Two students have identical recorded inputs. What does the same fixed rule predict for them?
answer: The same score. The calculation receives exactly the same numbers for both.

title: Slide 9 · By the end, you can follow the entire computation.
question: What would you compare to find out whether the score rule works on a new student?
answer: Compute the prediction from the study record, then compare it with that student’s observed score.

title: Slide 10 · Return to the Campus Study Coach.
question: Ava is one example. Name a feature and give its value for her.
answer: Study hours is a feature, and its value is 2. Completed practice sets is another, with value 3.

title: Slide 11 · What information do we need to make one prediction?
question: How could you store Ava’s two measurements so another person knows which is which?
answer: Use an ordered list [2, 3] and record the order as [hours, sets]. Reversing the labels changes what the numbers mean.

title: Slide 12 · Start with a list: one student, two numbers.
question: If we record sleep hours as a third feature, what is the shape of Ava’s list?
answer: It becomes (3,). There is still one axis, now with three entries.

title: Slide 13 · One student: a vector is not a column of students.
question: Does shape (2,) tell you which entry is study hours?
answer: The shape gives the length. You also need the feature order, here hours followed by sets.

title: Slide 14 · Count measurements, not students.
question: A student studied 3 hours and completed 4 practice sets. How many numbers are in the feature vector?
answer: Two measurements describe one student: [3, 4]. A 1D tensor with 2 entries has shape (2,).

title: Slide 15 · Stack several students into one table.
question: A fourth student joins the table. Which dimension grows?
answer: The row count increases from 3 to 4. With the same two features the shape becomes (4, 2).

title: Slide 16 · Three students: turn the spreadsheet into a matrix.
question: What does X[1, 0] select in this example?
answer: The second student’s first feature. Ben studied 4 hours, so the value is 4.

title: Slide 18 · Ask for one row—or just one column.
question: In X[:, 0], whose hours do we get?
answer: All three students’ hours. The colon selects every row and 0 selects the first column.

title: Slide 19 · Translate a classroom into a shape.
question: We record 5 students, each with 2 features. Which tensor shape describes the table?
answer: Five rows (students) and two columns (features) give shape (5, 2).

title: Slide 20 · A rule turns measurements into a predicted score.
question: What score does the rule predict for zero hours and zero sets?
answer: 20. Both weighted measurements contribute zero, leaving the starting score or bias.

title: Slide 21 · Let’s calculate Ava’s prediction together.
question: Which contributes more to Ava’s prediction, her hours or her sets?
answer: Hours contribute 2 × 10 = 20 points. Sets contribute 3 × 5 = 15 points.

title: Slide 22 · One operation scores all three students.
question: If X has eight rows and two columns, how many scores does X @ w + b return?
answer: Eight. The same two weights combine the two entries in each row into one score.

title: Slide 23 · Every prediction is the same weighted rule.
question: Why does multiplying a (3, 2) matrix by a length-two weight vector work?
answer: Each of the two entries per row has a matching weight. Adding their products gives one value per row.

title: Slide 25 · Predict a fourth student.
question: Our rule gives 10 points per hour + 5 per practice set + 20. What score does a student with 1 hour and 4 practice sets get?
answer: 20 + 10 + 20 = 50. This is a hand-chosen illustrative rule, not a valid actual grading model.

title: Slide 26 · Tensor operations transform the measurements.
question: After converting hours to minutes, what weight per minute preserves the score?
answer: 10/60 points per minute. Multiplying 120 minutes by 10/60 gives the same 20 points as two hours at 10.

title: Slide 27 · Changing units transforms values—not tensor rank.
question: Ava’s first entry goes from 2 to 120. Does that add another axis?
answer: No. It changes the unit and the value in one position. The table still has student rows and feature columns.

title: Slide 28 · Does changing units change shape?
question: Converting the hours column of a (3, 2) dataset from hours to minutes changes the tensor shape to what?
answer: Multiplying the values in one column by 60 changes their units, not the number of students or features.

title: Slide 29 · Add the same starting score to every student.
question: If the bias rises from 20 to 22, which predictions change?
answer: Each prediction rises by 2 because the same bias is added to every row.

title: Slide 30 · What if observations arrive every day?
question: What detail would disappear if we recorded only each student’s total weekly study hours?
answer: We could no longer tell which day the study happened. A day axis preserves that information.

title: Slide 31 · Add a day axis. You now have a stack of tables.
question: In a tensor ordered as student, day, feature, what remains after selecting one student and one day?
answer: One list of two features, the hours and practice sets for that student on that day.

title: Slide 32 · Three axes describe repeated measurements.
question: What does the middle 3 mean in (2, 3, 2)?
answer: There are three daily observations per student. The final 2 counts features per day.

title: Slide 33 · Average across the three days.
question: Ava studies 1, 2 and 3 hours on three days. What single value replaces those hours after averaging?
answer: 2 hours per day, since (1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2. The practice-set values are averaged separately.

title: Slide 34 · Averaging removes an axis.
question: Which averaging operation would combine different students’ records by mistake?
answer: Averaging over axis 0 combines students. For a separate average for each student, average over axis 1, the days.

title: Slide 35 · Where did the day axis go?
question: Two students × three days × two features has shape (2, 3, 2). If you average across days, what shape remains?
answer: The day axis disappears after mean(dim=1), leaving 2 students × 2 features.

title: Slide 36 · What if data is a picture?
question: What changes in (2, 1, 3, 3) if each picture has three color channels?
answer: The channel count changes from 1 to 3, giving (2, 3, 3, 3). There are still two pictures.

title: Slide 37 · In an image tensor, every axis has a physical meaning.
question: Why retain a channel axis of length one for grayscale?
answer: It identifies where channels belong in the same image layout used for color images.

title: Slide 38 · Turn each picture into a row of pixel measurements.
question: If each of two images has one channel, two rows and four columns, what is the flattened batch shape?
answer: Each image supplies 1 × 2 × 4 = 8 values. Keeping the two images separate gives (2, 8).

title: Slide 39 · Flatten pixels into features while retaining each student.
question: Can you tell from the length 9 alone whether an image was 3 by 3 or 1 by 9?
answer: No. Both layouts contain nine pixels. Save the original shape if you need to reconstruct the picture.

title: Slide 40 · What shape will flattening produce?
question: Two grayscale 3×3 images have shape (2, 1, 3, 3). After flatten(start_dim=1), what shape results?
answer: Each image contains 1 × 3 × 3 = 9 pixels, so the result is two rows of nine values.

title: Slide 41 · Add more independent axes as the data demands.
question: A third day is added for both students. Which length changes in (2, 2, 1, 3, 3)?
answer: The second length counts days. The new shape is (2, 3, 1, 3, 3).

title: Slide 42 · One new kind of observation means one more axis.
question: What does selecting one time index for every student leave?
answer: One image per student, with axes for student, channel, pixel row and pixel column.

title: Slide 43 · Rank tells you how many axes—not how much data.
question: Which has more axes, a list with 100 entries or a table with two rows and two columns?
answer: The table has two axes. The list has one axis even though it contains more entries.

title: Slide 44 · So far the parameters were chosen by hand.
question: Ava scores 60 after the rule predicts 55. Which numbers can training adjust?
answer: The weights and bias in the rule. Her recorded study activity and observed score supply the example used to judge the rule.

title: Slide 45 · Our initial predictions miss their targets.
question: What squared error comes from predicting 65 when the observed score is 60?
answer: The signed miss is 5. Squaring gives 25, the same penalty as a five-point miss in the other direction.

title: Slide 46 · Turn three prediction errors into one loss.
question: If the three errors are 0, 0 and 3, what is their mean squared error?
answer: The squared errors are 0, 0 and 9. Their mean is 9/3 = 3.

title: Slide 47 · Calculate the average squared error.
question: Predictions [55, 65, 80] and targets [60, 70, 75] have mean squared error equal to what?
answer: All squared errors equal 25, so the mean is also 25.

title: Slide 48 · Gradients show which direction should change.
question: After a small parameter update, the same batch’s loss changes from 25 to about 24.42. What can we conclude?
answer: The updated rule fits these three examples better according to this loss. We need fresh examples to assess performance on other students.

title: Slide 49 · The gradient connects mathematical learning to code.
question: Which part of an update controls how far we move for a given gradient?
answer: The learning rate scales the gradient. Doubling it doubles the proposed parameter change from the same starting point.

title: Slide 51 · This entire model is only a few lines of PyTorch.
question: What value is available after the prediction line but before loss.backward() runs?
answer: The predicted scores already exist. The backward call computes how the loss changes with each trainable parameter.

title: Slide 52 · Why does this matrix multiplication fail?
question: Can a (3, 2) dataset be multiplied by a length-3 weight vector using X @ w?
answer: Matrix multiplication (3, 2) @ (2,) is valid, producing (3,). The requested (3, 2) @ (3,) is not compatible.

title: Slide 53 · Machine learning is a pipeline of tensor operations.
question: Where in the sequence do the measured quiz scores first enter?
answer: They enter when we compare predictions with targets to calculate the loss.

title: Slide 54 · Keep learning with Virtual Office Hours.
question: You can compute an average, but your result has the wrong shape. What details would make a useful question?
answer: Include the input shape, what each axis counts, which axis you averaged, and the shape you obtained. Those details locate the step that needs explaining.

title: Slide 56 · From tensors to probability
question: A rule gives every student in a group a prediction of 55. Can you tell from that number alone what fraction will score above 60?
answer: No. The rule supplies a point prediction. To estimate the fraction above 60, we need information about how actual scores vary around it.

title: Office hours · Why is one student represented as a 1D tensor?
question: Why is one student represented as a 1D tensor?
answer: Start with Ava. We record 2 study hours and 3 practice sets, so her measurements are [2, 3]. It is one list with one axis: the feature position. Each position names a different measurement. There are two values, but that does not make it a 2D tensor. In machine learning, one example is often a feature vector.

title: Office hours · Why does a dataset with three students become 2D?
question: Why does a dataset with three students become 2D?
answer: Imagine three rows in a spreadsheet. Ava has [2,3], Ben [4,1], and Cam [5,2]. Stack these rows to form a table with three students and two features per student. The first axis chooses a student; the second chooses a measurement. Notice that dataset size and tensor rank are not the same thing.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between tensor rank and shape?
question: What is the difference between tensor rank and shape?
answer: Rank counts how many axes a tensor has. Shape tells us the length of each axis. Ava’s list has rank 1 and shape (2,). The entire class table has rank 2 and shape (3,2). A batch with one million rows can still have rank 2. In this course, “rank” means number of axes, not matrix rank from linear algebra.

title: Office hours · How do I select one row or one column from a dataset?
question: How do I select one row or one column from a dataset?
answer: In our three-student table, X[0] selects Ava’s entire row: her two measurements. X[:,0] means “every row, first column,” so it returns the study hours [2,4,5]. Python indexing begins at zero. A colon means all indices along that axis.

title: Office hours · What are model weights and the bias?
question: What are model weights and the bias?
answer: A parameterized function uses adjustable numbers to turn inputs into outputs. In our invented score rule, each study hour contributes 10 points, each practice set 5, and we add 20 baseline points. The two multipliers are weights; the starting term is a bias. They are hand-picked for demonstration. A trained model would estimate them from examples.

title: Office hours · Why does Ava get a predicted score of 55?
question: Why does Ava get a predicted score of 55?
answer: Ava studied 2 hours and completed 3 practice sets. Multiply each measurement by its matching weight: 2 × 10 = 20 and 3 × 5 = 15. Add the 20-point starting value. The prediction is 20 + 15 + 20 = 55. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a real educational prediction.

title: Office hours · How does one matrix multiplication predict scores for everyone?
question: How does one matrix multiplication predict scores for everyone?
answer: The class table has three rows, each containing two features. The weight vector contains two multipliers. Matrix–vector multiplication computes one weighted sum per row, producing three numbers. Adding the scalar bias 20 gives [55,65,80]. This is called vectorization: one operation applies the same rule to the entire class.

title: Office hours · How does Module 01 connect to linear algebra?
question: How does Module 01 connect to linear algebra?
answer:
Module 01 is an introduction to linear algebra through machine learning. Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies vectors, matrices, and the transformations we can perform with them. The module uses those ideas to answer a practical question: how can a computer represent many observations and apply the same prediction rule to all of them?

Think of a spreadsheet with one row per student and columns for study hours and practice sets. Read across one row: those measurements, in a fixed order, form a vector. Read the whole table: the rows and columns form a matrix. Now give each column a weight that says how much that measurement contributes to the prediction. Multiplying the matrix by the weight vector combines the measurements in each row and returns a vector of predicted contributions, one per student. Our model adds its starting score to each one.

That also explains why we introduce tensors here. In PyTorch, a one-dimensional tensor can hold a vector and a two-dimensional tensor can hold a matrix. When we record the same measurements over several days, a third axis keeps track of the day. The data still have a precise organization, and that organization tells us which calculations make sense. Later models can change the measurements and learn different weights while reusing these same ideas.

title: Office hours · What does broadcasting mean in our model?
question: What does broadcasting mean in our model?
answer: After multiplying the data table by the weight vector, we have one score per student: [35,45,60]. We want to add the same 20-point starting value to each. PyTorch broadcasts the scalar across all three values. It is not multiplying matrices, and it does not require us to type [20,20,20] ourselves.

title: Office hours · If we convert hours to minutes, what changes?
question: If we convert hours to minutes, what changes?
answer: Ava’s 2 hours become 120 minutes. The class still has three students and two features, so shape stays (3,2). But the numerical meaning changes! A model that expected hours cannot safely keep using the same 10-points-per-hour weight on values expressed in minutes. We must convert the corresponding weight or retrain.

title: Office hours · Why are daily logs a 3D tensor?
question: Why are daily logs a 3D tensor?
answer: Now each student reports measurements every day. We need to identify (1) which student, (2) which day, and (3) which measurement. For two students observed over three days with two features per day, the shape is (2,3,2). You can visualize this as two small tables stacked together. Each table has three rows (days) and two columns (measurements).

title: Office hours · What does mean(dim=1) do to the daily tensor?
question: What does mean(dim=1) do to the daily tensor?
answer: Axis 1 represents days (axis numbers start at zero). Averaging across days converts each student’s three daily records into one average record. We keep students and features but remove the day axis: shape changes from (2,3,2) to (2,2). For Ava, the averages are 2 study hours and 3 practice sets per day.

title: Office hours · Why does a batch of images have four axes?
question: Why does a batch of images have four axes?
answer: An individual grayscale picture is a 2D grid of pixel values. In our PyTorch convention, we also store a channel axis and a batch axis. Two tiny grayscale pictures of size 3 by 3 therefore have (student, channel, height, width) = (2,1,3,3). The number 4 refers to axes, not to picture size.

title: Office hours · What is flattening, and does it erase image information?
question: What is flattening, and does it erase image information?
answer: Flattening lists pixels from each picture in one long row. Our 2 images × 1 channel × 3 rows × 3 columns become 2 images × 9 pixel features. No numerical pixel value disappears; however, the explicit row-and-column structure is no longer visible in the shape. This matters when choosing between a simple dense model and a convolutional model.

title: Office hours · What would a 5D tensor mean?
question: What would a 5D tensor mean?
answer: Suppose we save two image snapshots per student instead of one. We now need student, time, channel, height, and width: five axes. With two students, two times, one grayscale channel, and 3×3 images, the tensor has shape (2,2,1,3,3). Higher tensor rank simply reflects additional kinds of indexing.

title: Office hours · What makes this a learning system rather than a fixed formula?
question: What makes this a learning system rather than a fixed formula?
answer: So far we chose the model weights manually and applied the same rule. Learning starts when we also have target outputs and adjust the parameters to reduce a loss measuring prediction error. PyTorch can track how a loss depends on the weights and calculate gradients. An optimizer then uses those gradients to update the model. Simply computing predictions is inference; changing parameters from evidence is training.

title: Office hours · How do we compute mean squared error in this example?
question: How do we compute mean squared error in this example?
answer: Our predicted toy scores are [55,65,80], while fictional targets are [60,70,75]. The errors are [−5,−5,+5]. Squaring gives [25,25,25]. Averaging the three squared errors gives 25. The square means errors in either direction are penalized, and larger errors have stronger effect.

title: Office hours · What is a gradient, and how do the weights change?
question: What is a gradient, and how do the weights change?
answer: Think of the loss as measuring how poorly our current model fits the three examples. A gradient tells us how the loss changes for a small change in each parameter. PyTorch uses backward() to compute those derivatives from the recorded operations. With a small learning rate, we subtract a fraction of each gradient. In our numerical toy example, one update reduces mean squared error from 25 to approximately 24.42.

title: Office hours · Why does X @ w fail if my weights have the wrong length?
question: Why does X @ w fail if my weights have the wrong length?
answer: Our dataset has two features in every row, so each output needs one weight per feature. X has shape (3,2): three examples and two measurements each. A length-3 weight vector does not match the two feature slots. Matrix multiplication checks these inner dimensions; use a length-2 weight vector to produce three predictions.

title: Office hours · How do I read X ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ and ŷ = Xw + b?
question: How do I read X ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ and ŷ = Xw + b?
answer: Read X ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ as “X is a real-valued table with n rows and d columns.” In our story n=3 students and d=2 features. Read w ∈ ℝᵈ as “one weight per feature.” Then ŷ = Xw + b means “compute a weighted sum for each student, and add the shared bias.” In formal papers, symbols compress a concrete computational story. Always annotate axes and dimensions before manipulating the equation.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between elementwise multiplication and a dot product?
question: What is the difference between elementwise multiplication and a dot product?
answer: Elementwise multiplication makes a new list of products. For Ava, [2,3] × [10,5] becomes [20,15]. The dot product then adds those products into a single number: 20+15=35. Adding the bias gives 55. In PyTorch, the star operator multiplies element by element, while torch.dot or @ contracts the matching feature axis.

title: Exercise 9
question: If you have 4 students, 7 days, and 3 measurements per day, what is the rank of the tensor?
answer: Student, day, and measurement are three independent axes; shape is (4, 7, 3), rank 3.

title: Exercise 10
question: If we record 2 daily image snapshots per student, adding time to (2, 1, 3, 3), what is the new 5D shape under (student, day, channel, height, width)?
answer: Five axes: 2 students, 2 days, 1 grayscale channel, 3 pixel rows, 3 pixel columns.
